question.prompt:
Let \(h_n\) and \(k_n\) be the unique relatively prime positive integers such that

\[\frac11+\frac12+\frac13+\cdots+\frac1n=\frac{h_n}{k_n}.\]

Let \(L_n\) denote the least common multiple of the numbers \(1,\) \(2,\) \(3,\) \(\ldots,\) \(n.\) For how many integers \(n\) with \(1\le n\le22\) is \(k_n\lt L_n?\)

solutions.title: Test cancellation prime by prime
solutions.explanation:
Writing the sum over the denominator \(L_n\) lets us test whether any prime factor cancels. Define the integer
\[
N_n=\sum_{j=1}^n\frac{L_n}{j}.
\]
Then
\[
k_n=\frac{L_n}{\gcd(N_n,L_n)},
\]
so we need a prime dividing both \(N_n\) and \(L_n\).

Fix a prime \(p\le n\), and let \(q=p^a\) be its largest power not exceeding \(n\). The prime factorization of \(L_n\) contains exactly this power of \(p\). Thus \(L_n/j\) is divisible by \(p\) unless \(j\) is a multiple of \(q\).

Put \(t=\lfloor n/q\rfloor\). Since \(pq>n\), we have \(t<p\). The only terms that matter modulo \(p\) therefore have denominators
\[
q,2q,\ldots,tq.
\]
Let \(B=L_n/q\), which is not divisible by \(p\). Their sum is
\[
B\left(1+\frac12+\cdots+\frac1t\right).
\]
Write the parenthesized sum in lowest terms as \(u/v\). Each \(j\le t\) divides \(B\), so \(v\) divides \(B\). Consequently, the displayed sum is \((B/v)u\), where \(B/v\) is an integer not divisible by \(p\). We conclude that \(p\) cancels precisely when \(p\mid u\).

For \(n\le22\), the values of \(t\) needed are at most \(4\):

| \(t\) | \(1+1/2+\cdots+1/t\) | Reduced numerator |
|---|---|---|
| \(1\) | \(1\) | \(1\) |
| \(2\) | \(3/2\) | \(3\) |
| \(3\) | \(11/6\) | \(11\) |
| \(4\) | \(25/12\) | \(25\) |

We can now check every prime at most \(22\):

| Prime \(p\) | Possible largest powers \(q\) | Possible \(t\) | Values of \(n\) where \(p\) cancels |
|---|---|---|---|
| \(2\) | \(2,4,8,16\) | \(1\) | None |
| \(3\) | \(3,9\) | \(1,2\) | \(6,7,8,18,19,20,21,22\) |
| \(5\) | \(5\) | \(1,2,3,4\) | \(20,21,22\) |
| \(7\) | \(7\) | \(1,2,3\) | None |
| \(11\) | \(11\) | \(1,2\) | None |
| \(13,17,19\) | \(p\) | \(1\) | None |

For example, \(3\) cancels when \(t=2\): this means \(6\le n\le8\) for \(q=3\), or \(18\le n\le22\) for \(q=9\). Similarly, \(5\) cancels only when \(t=4\), giving \(20\le n\le22\). These last three values have already been counted. At \(n=1\), both denominators equal \(1\).

Thus the qualifying integers are
\[
6,7,8,18,19,20,21,22,
\]
for a total of \(\boxed{8}\), choice \(\boxed{\text{D}}\).

solutions.title: Build the fractions recursively
solutions.explanation:
There are only \(22\) sums to check, so an exact recurrence gives a direct route using fraction arithmetic. Keep each sum over its least common denominator by writing
\[
1+\frac12+\cdots+\frac1n=\frac{N_n}{L_n},
\]
without reducing the fraction.

Starting with \(L_1=N_1=1\), adding \(1/n\) gives
\[
L_n=\operatorname{lcm}(L_{n-1},n),
\qquad
N_n=\frac{L_n}{L_{n-1}}N_{n-1}+\frac{L_n}{n}.
\]
Both terms on the right are integers. If \(d_n=\gcd(N_n,L_n)\), then reducing the fraction gives \(k_n=L_n/d_n\). Thus a row qualifies exactly when \(d_n>1\).

For example, \(L_6=60\) and
\[
N_6=137+\frac{60}{6}=147,
\qquad
\gcd(147,60)=3.
\]
Applying the recurrence throughout the requested range gives:

| \(n\) | \(L_n\) | \(N_n\) | \(d_n\) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | 1 | 1 | 1 |
| 2 | 2 | 3 | 1 |
| 3 | 6 | 11 | 1 |
| 4 | 12 | 25 | 1 |
| 5 | 60 | 137 | 1 |
| 6 | 60 | 147 | 3 |
| 7 | 420 | 1089 | 3 |
| 8 | 840 | 2283 | 3 |
| 9 | 2520 | 7129 | 1 |
| 10 | 2520 | 7381 | 1 |
| 11 | 27720 | 83711 | 1 |
| 12 | 27720 | 86021 | 1 |
| 13 | 360360 | 1145993 | 1 |
| 14 | 360360 | 1171733 | 1 |
| 15 | 360360 | 1195757 | 1 |
| 16 | 720720 | 2436559 | 1 |
| 17 | 12252240 | 42142223 | 1 |
| 18 | 12252240 | 42822903 | 3 |
| 19 | 232792560 | 825887397 | 3 |
| 20 | 232792560 | 837527025 | 15 |
| 21 | 232792560 | 848612385 | 45 |
| 22 | 232792560 | 859193865 | 45 |

The rows with \(d_n>1\) are \(n=6,7,8,18,19,20,21,22\). Hence the answer is \(\boxed{8}\), choice \(\boxed{\text{D}}\).
